name: Kumaon
tagline: Lakes, oak ridges and the old Tibet road
meta_description: Plan Kumaon in Uttarakhand: Nainital lakes, Almora and Kasar Devi, Binsar, Jageshwar, Kausani and Munsiyari, with honest saver, comfort and signature trips.
summary: Kumaon is the eastern half of Uttarakhand: lake towns near Kathgodam, the old Chand capital of Almora, oak sanctuaries like Binsar, the stone temples of Jageshwar and the Johar valley at Munsiyari. Go March to June or September to November. Five to nine nights by train, shared jeep or private car covers the best of it.
intro: Kumaon starts where the plains stop. The railway ends at Kathgodam, 625 m above sea level, and within an hour the road has climbed to Bhimtal and Nainital, two of the lakes that gave this district its old name, the land of sixty lakes. Beyond them the hills fold north in ridges of banj oak, chir pine and deodar, each ridge with a temple on top and terraced villages on the warm southern slope.

The Chand kings ruled from Almora from the 1560s, and their town is still the cultural centre of the hive: copper workers, the bal mithai sweet shops of Lal Bazaar, aipan patterns painted on doorsteps. Twenty kilometres away the Binsar sanctuary protects oak forest where the Chands kept a summer seat, and Jageshwar hides more than a hundred stone temples in a deodar valley.

Further north the snow peaks come close. Kausani looks across 300 km of the range from Trishul to Panchachuli, and the road beyond Bageshwar and Thal climbs to Munsiyari, the winter home of the Johari Shauka traders who once took mule trains over the passes to Tibet. From here the Johar valley runs up to Milam glacier.

We plan Kumaon at three levels. Saver trips use the overnight train, Uttarakhand Roadways and KMOU buses, shared jeeps, KMVN rest houses and hostels. Comfort trips add a private car with driver and good heritage hotels. Signature trips use the few small hotels here that are worth the drive, with a private naturalist or guide. Check current status before you travel in the monsoon.

story.title: Kings, salt traders and seekers on the ridge

chapters.heading: From Katyuri temples to the Chand court
chapters.text: Before Almora there was Katyur. The Katyuri kings ruled much of this country from the Garur and Baijnath valley, and the stone temples at Baijnath and Jageshwar, built between roughly the 7th and 14th centuries, are their best surviving record. When Katyuri power broke apart, the Chand dynasty slowly gathered the hills under one court. In the 1560s they moved their capital to Almora, a saddle of land above the Kosi, and built the palaces whose sites now hold the town's collectorate and hospital. In 1688 King Udyot Chand raised temples in Almora to mark victories over Garhwal and Doti. Gorkha armies took Kumaon in 1790, and after the Anglo-Nepalese war of 1814 to 1816 it passed to the British.

chapters.heading: Salt, wool and the Johar passes
chapters.text: In the far north-east, the Johar valley of the Gori Ganga was a trading corridor. The Johari Shauka, part of the wider Bhotiya community, spent summer in high villages such as Milam, above 3,000 m, and crossed the Untadhura and nearby passes to the Tibetan market at Gyanima with grain and goods, returning with salt and wool. In winter the snow closed Milam and families walked down to Munsiyari. Nain Singh Rawat, born in Milam in 1830, used that knowledge of Tibet to become one of the British survey's pundit explorers and fixed the position of Lhasa. The 1962 war ended the Johar trade, and the valley's families have since moved mostly to Munsiyari and the plains.

chapters.heading: Lake towns of the Raj
chapters.text: Nainital was a hunting ground until 1841, when the sugar trader P. Barron built the first European house by the lake. It grew into the summer capital of the United Provinces, and its history still turns on the landslip of 18 September 1880, which buried 151 people and the old Naina Devi temple; the Flats were built on the debris. The British set up a cantonment at Ranikhet in 1869, now home of the Kumaon Regiment, and moved a cattle-plague serum laboratory to Mukteshwar in 1893, today the Indian Veterinary Research Institute. Jim Corbett grew up between Nainital and his winter house at Kaladhungi, and later wrote about the man-eaters of these hills.

chapters.heading: Seekers on the ridge
chapters.text: Kumaon has a long record of visitors who came to think. Swami Vivekananda meditated at Kasar Devi in the 1890s. In June 1929 Mahatma Gandhi spent about two weeks at Kausani, writing his commentary on the Gita called Anasakti Yoga; the house is now the Anasakti Ashram. From the 1930s Western Buddhists and writers settled on the pine ridge beyond Kasar Devi, and in the 1960s Allen Ginsberg, Gary Snyder and Timothy Leary came to visit, giving it the name Crank's Ridge. In 1964 Neem Karoli Baba consecrated the Hanuman temple at Kainchi Dham near Bhowali, which now draws millions of pilgrims a year.

highlights.title: A dawn row on Naini lake
highlights.text: Nainital's lake is 1,433 m long and sits at about 1,938 m. At 6 am, before the Mall fills, a hand-rowed boat across to the Naina Devi temple on the north shore costs a few hundred rupees and shows the town as the Raj built it, hill by hill.

highlights.title: Almora's Lal Bazaar and Kasar Devi
highlights.text: Walk the stone-paved Lal Bazaar of the old Chand capital for bal mithai and singori, then take a shared taxi 8 km up to Kasar Devi. The pine ridge beyond the temple, called Crank's Ridge, hosted Buddhist scholars in the 1930s and Beat poets in the 1960s.

highlights.title: Binsar's oak forest
highlights.text: Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary protects 45.6 sq km of banj oak and rhododendron forest, set up in 1988. Walk 2 km from the KMVN rest house to Zero Point at about 2,400 m for a 300 km line of peaks, from Chaukhamba to Panchachuli, on a clear October morning.

highlights.title: Jageshwar's stone temples
highlights.text: In a deodar valley 36 km from Almora stand more than a hundred cut-stone temples, mostly to Shiva, built between about the 7th and 14th centuries and looked after by the Archaeological Survey of India. Come at 7 am, when the evening's ghee lamps are still being cleaned.

highlights.title: Gandhi's two weeks in Kausani
highlights.text: Kausani sits on a 1,890 m ridge with a wide view of Trishul and Nanda Devi. Gandhi stayed here in June 1929 and wrote Anasakti Yoga; the house is now the Anasakti Ashram, with a small exhibition and a prayer hall open to visitors.

highlights.title: Munsiyari and the Johar valley
highlights.text: At about 2,200 m, Munsiyari faces the five summits of Panchachuli across the Gori valley. It was the winter home of the Johari Shauka traders of Milam. Hike to Khaliya Top, see the Tribal Heritage Museum, and ask about permits for the Milam glacier trek.

money_savers: Take the overnight Ranikhet Express from Delhi to Kathgodam: a sleeper or 3AC berth costs less than a taxi and saves a hotel night.
Avoid Nainital on long weekends and from mid-May to mid-June, when room rates on the Mall can double; Bhowali, Bhimtal and Sattal are calmer and cheaper.
Use Uttarakhand Roadways and KMOU buses or shared jeeps from Haldwani and Kathgodam; a seat to Almora costs a fraction of a private cab.
Book KMVN tourist rest houses on the official KMVN site; at Binsar and Kausani they are among the best-sited rooms in town for the price.
Eat Kumaoni thalis at local dhabas for ₹150–250 instead of hotel buffets, and buy bal mithai by weight in Almora rather than in gift boxes elsewhere.
Travel from late September to early November: clear views, open roads and shoulder prices outside the Diwali week.
getting_there: Most travellers reach Kumaon through Kathgodam, the railhead below Nainital. The New Delhi–Kathgodam Shatabdi runs by day in about six hours, and the overnight Ranikhet Express and Uttarakhand Sampark Kranti also reach Kathgodam from Delhi. Haldwani, 6 km south, is the main bus and shared-jeep hub, with Uttarakhand Roadways buses from Delhi's Anand Vihar ISBT in about 7–9 hours and KMOU buses into the hills. Pantnagar Airport, about 70 km from Nainital, has a small number of flights from Delhi and a few other cities. From Kathgodam it is about 35 km to Nainital, 90 km to Almora and around 280 km to Munsiyari. Check current status before you travel, as train timings and flights change.
permits: Most of Kumaon needs no permit for Indian or foreign visitors. Inner Line rules apply near the Tibet border: the upper Johar valley beyond Munsiyari towards Milam, and the Darma and Vyans valleys towards Adi Kailash and Om Parvat. Indian nationals apply for an Inner Line Permit through the SDM office (Munsiyari or Dharchula) with ID and a medical certificate where asked; foreign nationals face tighter limits. Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary charges an entry fee at its gate. Check current status before you travel, as border rules change.

months.weather: Nainital about 2 to 11 °C; frost, occasional snow above 2,000 m
months.summary: Cold, clear and quiet. Mornings in Nainital and Mukteshwar can drop near freezing, and a western disturbance may bring snow to Mukteshwar, Binsar and Munsiyari for a day or two. Views of the high peaks are often the sharpest of the year. Hotels discount outside the New Year week, and roads to Munsiyari may close briefly after heavy snow. Pack thermals and expect early sunsets around 5:30 pm.
months.tip: If you want snow, watch the forecast for a western disturbance and head for Mukteshwar a day after it passes.

months.summary: Still wintry at night but the days lengthen. Early rhododendron blooms appear on the lower slopes late in the month. Few tourists, so KMVN rooms and heritage hotels are easy to book. It is a good month for Jageshwar and Almora, where the temples are quiet and the light is clear. Snow is possible at Munsiyari, so check the road via Thal before you set out.
months.tip: Carry cash for Binsar's gate fee and for village dhabas, as card machines are rare.

months.weather: Nainital about 6 to 17 °C; spring hail possible
months.summary: Buransh flowers turn the oak forests of Binsar, Mukteshwar and Chaukori red, and buransh squash appears in shops. Days are mild, nights cool, and the snow line is still low enough for good mountain views. Holi week brings Kumaoni baithki holi singing in Almora and Nainital homes and halls. Hailstorms can hit in the afternoon, so plan walks for the morning.
months.tip: Book Holi week early in Almora if you want to hear the baithki holi song sessions.

months.summary: One of the best months. Rhododendrons peak above 2,000 m, the air is warm by day, and birding at Sattal and Binsar is at its best as breeding species call. Haze from the plains and forest fires can soften the mountain views later in the month. School holidays have not started, so rooms are still reasonably priced outside weekends.
months.tip: Start birding walks at first light; by 10 am the forest goes quiet.

months.summary: Peak season. Families from the plains fill Nainital, Bhimtal and Ranikhet, and traffic on the Kathgodam road can stall for hours on weekends. Kafal berries appear by the roadside. Higher places such as Munsiyari and Chaukori are pleasant and less crowded. Book stays and the Shatabdi weeks ahead and leave early in the day.
months.tip: In Nainital, use the shuttle and park outside town; private cars face long waits at peak hours.

months.weather: Nainital about 14 to 24 °C; pre-monsoon showers late
months.summary: The first half is busy and warm; the monsoon usually reaches Kumaon in the second half of June. Kainchi Dham's foundation-day mela on 15 June draws very large crowds and traffic controls on the Bhowali–Almora road. After the rains start, landslides begin to close roads for hours at a time. Good for higher places early in the month.
months.tip: Avoid driving past Kainchi Dham around 15 June unless you are going to the mela.

months.weather: Heavy monsoon rain; Nainital about 16 to 23 °C
months.summary: The wettest month. Clouds hide the peaks, leeches appear on forest trails, and landslides block roads to Munsiyari, Chaukori and beyond Almora, sometimes for days. Harela, the green festival, falls in mid-July, and Jageshwar's Shravan month draws pilgrims. Travel only with spare days and flexible bookings. Check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Keep a buffer day before any train home; landslides on the Kathgodam road are common.

months.summary: Still monsoon. Forests are green, waterfalls run full and prices are low, but views are rare and road closures frequent. Jageshwar's Shravan festivities continue into August, and in some years the Nanda Devi Mela in Almora and Nainital begins at the end of the month. Lake towns close to Kathgodam are the safest choice.
months.tip: Check road status each morning with your hotel or the district disaster control room before setting out.

months.summary: The monsoon weakens through the month and the air clears from late September. The Nanda Devi Mela fills Almora and Nainital with processions and stalls, depending on the lunar date. Roads may still be under repair after the rains, so allow time. Hotels are still at low-season rates in the first half.
months.tip: The second half of September is often the cheapest time to get October-quality views.

months.summary: The best month for mountain views. The full line of peaks shows from Binsar, Kausani, Chaukori and Munsiyari most mornings. Days are dry, nights cool, and treks to Pindari and Khaliya Top are in good shape. Durga Puja and Diwali holidays push up prices for a week or so; book those weeks early.
months.tip: Be at Zero Point in Binsar or the Kausani viewpoint 20 minutes before sunrise.

months.summary: Clear, cold mornings and quiet roads. Views stay excellent and crowds thin after Diwali. The Kasar Devi fair falls on Kartik Purnima. Munsiyari gets cold, below freezing at night, but the Panchachuli views are at their best. A good month for slow, writing or workation trips at Kasar Devi and Mukteshwar.
months.tip: Carry a down jacket for dawn viewpoints; it is often near 0 °C at 2,200 m.

months.weather: Nainital about 2 to 13 °C; cold, mostly dry
months.summary: Cold and mostly dry with clear views. The Christmas and New Year week is busy and expensive in Nainital, Bhimtal and Mukteshwar; the rest of the month is quiet. Snow is possible late in the month above 2,000 m. Short days mean less driving time, so plan fewer, shorter legs.
months.tip: Book New Year week by October or skip it; mid-December is far better value.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kumaon?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest views of Trishul, Nanda Devi and Panchachuli, with dry roads and cool nights. March to mid-June is good for rhododendrons and birding, though May and early June are crowded in Nainital. July and August bring heavy monsoon rain and landslides. December to February is cold but clear, with occasional snow above 2,000 m.

faqs.q: How do I reach Kumaon from Delhi?
faqs.a: Take a train to Kathgodam: the Shatabdi by day (about six hours) or the overnight Ranikhet Express. Uttarakhand Roadways buses run from Anand Vihar ISBT to Haldwani, Nainital and Almora. By car, Delhi to Nainital is about 320 km and 7–9 hours via Moradabad and Rampur. Pantnagar Airport has a few flights from Delhi. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Kumaon?
faqs.a: Three nights covers Nainital and Bhimtal on a weekend from Delhi. Five to six nights adds Almora, Kasar Devi and Binsar or Jageshwar. Eight to ten nights lets you reach Kausani, Chaukori and Munsiyari without long days. Munsiyari alone needs at least three nights there because the drive from Kathgodam takes 9–11 hours.

faqs.q: How much does a budget trip to Kumaon cost?
faqs.a: A careful traveller spends ₹1,800–3,000 a day per person: ₹500–900 for a hostel bed or ₹1,500–2,500 for a shared double, ₹400–700 for food at dhabas, and ₹200–600 for buses or shared jeeps. A five-night saver trip from Kathgodam costs about ₹13,000–18,000 per person, plus your train from Delhi.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Kumaon?
faqs.a: No permit is needed for Nainital, Almora, Binsar, Jageshwar, Kausani, Ranikhet, Chaukori or Munsiyari town. Inner Line Permits apply to the upper Johar valley towards Milam and to the Vyans valley towards Adi Kailash and Om Parvat, issued through SDM offices in Munsiyari and Dharchula. Binsar sanctuary charges a gate fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Kumaon safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Kumaon is generally considered safe and its towns are used to solo travellers, especially Almora, Kasar Devi and Munsiyari. Usual care applies: avoid driving or walking forest roads after dark, use registered taxis, and tell your stay your plans. Hostels at Kasar Devi and Mukteshwar have mixed and women-only dorms. Leopards live near many towns, another reason not to walk alone at night.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and ATM access in Kumaon?
faqs.a: Jio, Airtel and BSNL work in Nainital, Bhimtal, Almora, Ranikhet, Kausani and Munsiyari town. Signal is weak or absent inside Binsar sanctuary and at points along the Thal–Munsiyari road. ATMs are found in district towns such as Haldwani, Nainital, Almora, Ranikhet, Bageshwar and Munsiyari but can run out of cash on holidays, so carry enough for two or three days.

faqs.q: Is Kumaon good for families with children and seniors?
faqs.a: Yes. Most stays are between 1,300 m and 2,200 m, so altitude is not a concern for healthy travellers, and the lake towns near Kathgodam are a short drive from the railhead. The hard part is winding roads: carry motion-sickness tablets, plan drives under five hours, and choose stays with few steps. Talk to your doctor about long drives for seniors with heart conditions.

Its lakes around Nainital, the old Chand capital of Almora, the hilltop views of Kausani and Binsar, the Jageshwar temple group, and Munsiyari's Panchachuli view. Locally it is known for bal mithai and singori sweets, aipan floor art, Kumaoni holi songs, copperwork in Almora, and the Johar valley's trade history with Tibet.
